paper_title: DEPICT: Scoring Text-to-Image Alignment by Answer Agreement

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Image-text alignment is a core problem in computer vision with applications in caption evaluation, hallucination detection, data curation, and the benchmarking of text-to-image (T2I) generators. As T2I models improve, benchmarking has become demanding, requiring metrics capable of finding a series of issues like missing objects, swapped attributes, miscounts, and ignored negations. Recent work addresses this by fine-tuning evaluators on preference data or by prompting a vision-language model, either holistically with the caption or with decomposed verification questions. However, existing approaches fall short: fine-tuned metrics remain bound to one backbone and training distribution; holistic metrics miss fine-grained details; and decomposed metrics rely on a fixed-YES assumption that penalizes faithful images whenever that assumption fails. In contrast, we propose DEPICT, a training-free metric that replaces fixed reference answers with expected agreement between image-based and caption-only answers, weighting questions by how decisively the caption determines them. By replacing fixed references, our agreement rule increases negation accuracy from 19% to 88%. To recover the context lost during decomposition, DEPICT merges this agreement score with a holistic score. We evaluate DEPICT on five benchmarks and eleven backbones from three model families and find that it surpasses all training-free metrics and exceeds fine-tuned evaluators on two out of three human-correlation benchmarks.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Image-text alignment evaluation is fundamental across vision-language tasks, including caption scoring (Hessel et al., 2021), vision-language models (VLM) hallucination detection (Kogilathota et al., 2026), data filtering (Schuhmann et al., 2021; Gadre et al., 2023), and, increasingly, evaluating text-to-image (T2I) generators (Kamath et al., 2025; Ramos et al., 2026) and their reward signals (Xu et al., 2023; Black et al., 2024). As T2I models improve, the question has shifted from whether they can generate an image that matches prompt to whether they can render every aspect of it faithfully, without dropping an object, swapping an attribute, miscounting, or ignoring negation (Labs et al., 2025; Chefer et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). An alignment metric must therefore correlate with human judgments on open-ended text, including these fine-grained errors (Ku et al., 2024). Two families of evaluators have emerged. Fine-tuned metrics learn scoring function from preference data (Xu et al., 2023; Kirstain et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Marjit et al., 2026), while training-free ones prompt an off-the-shelf VLM (Lin et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2023; Cho et al., 2024). We focus on the trainingfree family due to fundamental structural advantage: while fine-tuned evaluators remain bound to specific architecture and the static distribution of their training data, training-free metrics naturally scale alongside foundation models, inheriting backbone advancements without task-specific re-training. To evaluate how effectively these metrics leverage underlying backbone improvements, we conduct what is, to our knowledge, the first study assessing them across eleven backbones from three model families and five benchmarks. Within the training-free family, two approaches have developed separately. Holistic scoring started with global embedding similarity between separately encoded text and image (Hessel et al., 2021) and newer approaches ask VLMs single question about the whole caption and read the probability of yes (Lin et al. (2024); Figure 1a). Decomposed scoring methods generate set of verification questions from the caption, answer each against the image, and aggregate the results to obtain final score (Hu et al. (2023); Cho et al. (2024); Kamath et al. (2025); Figure 1b). Holistic scoring preserves macro context and decomposed metrics offer fine-grained interpretability, but neither approach dominates across benchmarks. Decomposed metrics also share flaw in how each answer is scored. Later methods simplified this by assuming constant yes target, scored either by hard string matches (Cho et al., 2024) or their probabilities (Kamath et al., 2025). We call this the fixed-yes assumption: the expected answer is fixed before looking at the image, so whenever it is wrong, the metric fails with it. We propose Depict, training-free alignment metric (Figure 1c). Given caption, Depict decomposes the description into set of visual assertions without requiring ground-truth labels. VLM evaluates each assertion twice, once against the image and once against the caption alone, assigning verdict to each. The score reflects the agreement between the two channels, which is high whenever both favor the same truth value, regardless of polarity. We further find that the holistic and decomposed paradigms are complementary rather than competing and Depict is the first metric to merge them. Across every human-judgment benchmark we test, the merged score correlates better with human ratings than either approach alone. Our contributions are: Diagnosis of the fixed-yes flaw. We uncover fundamental structural flaw in current decomposed metrics, the fixed-yes assumption, which causes their accuracy on negated prompts to drop below chance. Agreement-based scoring. We score each question by the agreement between text-only and visual answer, which removes the assumption and improves both negation accuracy and correlation with human judgements. Systematic benchmark study. We present, to our knowledge, the first comparison of training-free T2I alignment metrics across backbones from several model families and multiple benchmarks, with paired confidence intervals for every difference. Depict. We merge agreement-based decomposed scoring with holistic scoring in training-free metric. It exceeds the strongest fine-tuned evaluator on its own backbone on most human-judgment benchmarks and consistently matches or beats training-free baselines across backbones and benchmarks.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Embedding-based metrics. Early alignment metrics like CLIPScore (Hessel et al., 2021) and BLIP2Score (Li et al., 2023) rely on global image-text similarity. Because these models are pre-trained for coarse caption matching rather than fine-grained relational reasoning, they behave as bag-of-words matchers (Yüksekgönül et al., 2023; Koishigarina et al., 2026) that struggle with compositionality and correlate weakly with human judgments (Hu et al., 2023; Cho et al., 2024). Fine-tuned metrics. The initial approaches take the encoders above and align their outputs with human preference data (Xu et al., 2023; Kirstain et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023), while newer evaluators start from VLM and learn from human ratings or from larger teacher model (Tu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Marjit et al., 2026). In both cases, the learned score is bound to its backbone and its training data. DynEval (Marjit et al., 2026), the strongest of these, fine-tunes decomposition pipeline on Qwen3-VL (Yang et al., 2025) and serves as our matched-backbone reference. Training-free metrics. These metrics query an off-the-shelf VLM (Yang et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026), so any stronger backbone can be swapped in at no cost. sections.title: 3 Measuring Alignment Between Text and Vision
sections.content: We present Depict, training-free metric that scores an image against caption t. Rather than scoring each question against fixed answer as prior decomposed metrics do (Hu et al., 2023; Cho et al., 2024), Depict treats the answer {yes, no} as latent variable. It generates questions directly from the caption, answers each from the image and from the caption alone, and scores question by the probability that the two answers coincide, marginalized over both outcomes. Questions are then weighted by how decisively the caption settles them, and the resulting decomposed score is merged with holistic one (Figure 2). Generating questions from the caption. DSG (Cho et al., 2024) first parses into semantic tuples and then converts each tuple into question. We skip the intermediate parsing step by prompting language model to produce yes/no questions {qk}N directly from , each targeting single verifiable detail and answerable from the image alone. Unlike DSG, the generator sees the whole caption, so questions do not inherit possible parsing errors and retain the context that tuple extraction discards, making post-hoc filtering and dependency graph unnecessary. sections.title: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Datasets, metrics, and statistics. To measure the correlation with human judgements, we use GenAIBench (Li et al., 2024), TIFA160 (Hu et al., 2023), and RichHF-18K (Liang et al., 2024) misalignment_score, reporting Spearman Rank Correlation Coefficient (SRCC) on raw scores and Pearson Linear Correlation Coefficient (PLCC) following Han et al. (2024). For diagnostics, we use Winoground (Thrush et al., 2022), reporting text, image, and group accuracy, and the COCO-MCQ split of NegBench (Alhamoud et al., 2025). Score differences () between metrics is paired, with BCa 95% intervals over = 10,000 bootstrap replicates resampled by item. Dataset details are presented in Appendix A.1. Baselines. We compare against three groups of metrics. 1) Training-free, embedding-similarity metrics score the cosine similarity of caption and image embeddings from contrastive encoder: CLIPScore (Hessel et al., 2021) and BLIPv2Score (Li et al., 2023). 2) Training-free, VLM-based metrics prompt an off-the-shelf VLM and run on any backbone; these are the focus of our analysis, and we take one representative per cell of the decomposition granularity grid of Section 5.2: DSG (Cho et al., 2024) (decomposed, discrete), Soft-TIFA (Kamath et al., 2025) (decomposed, continuous; the Faith rule of Eq. 1), and VQAScore (Lin et al., 2024) (holistic, continuous). 3) Fine-tuned evaluators learn scoring function from preference data or teacher annotations and are tied to their training backbone: ImageReward (Xu et al., 2023), PickScore (Kirstain et al., 2023), UniGenBench++ (Wang et al., 2026), LongT2IBench (Yang et al., 2026), T2I-Eval (Tu et al., 2025), FGA-BLIP2 (Han et al., 2024), and DynEval (Marjit et al., 2026). Backbones. To decouple the scoring procedure from visual reasoning capability, all training-free methods are run on eleven backbones varying along four axes: 1) family, via Qwen3.5 (Yang et al., 2025), InternVL3.5 (Wang et al., 2025), and Gemma-4 (Team et al., 2026); 2) scale, via two size ladders (Qwen3.5 4B/9B/27B, InternVL3.5 4B/8B/14B); 3) generation, via Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 at fixed 27B; and 4) architecture, via the Gemma-4 variants (per-layer embedding E4B, unified multimodal 12B, dense 31B). sections.title: 5 Results and Discussion
sections.content: We evaluate Depict against fine-tuned and training-free baselines across human alignment, compositional discrimination, and explicit negation. Across five benchmarks and eleven backbones, we show that expected agreement and term merging match or exceed fine-tuned evaluators, hold across backbones, and avoid failures of fixed-yes metrics. Qualitative evaluation is provided in Appendix E.

sections.title: 5.2 Where do the gains come from?
sections.content: To separate procedure from backbone capability, Table 2 fixes the backbone at Qwen3.5-27B, so trainingfree methods differ only in how they score. The rows map onto the components of Section 3: DSG uses its own tuple-based questions with hard scoring, Soft-TIFA-AM scores our questions with Faith, VQAScore is the holistic term, and Depicts decomposed term scores the same questions with Agree before being merged with holistic term. The baselines split by benchmark. Comparing training-free baselines on shared backbone reveals neither paradigm dominates. Soft-TIFA leads on TIFA160, whereas VQAScore leads on GenAI-Bench and RichHF  (Table 2)  . TIFA160 favors decomposition in general, with decomposed metrics scoring 0.09-0.22 higher on TIFA160 than on GenAI-Bench (against 0.04 for VQAScore) which is pattern consistent across every decomposed evaluator in Table 1, fine-tuned or not. The decomposed term closes the gap to holistic scoring. Switching the scoring rule from Faith (SoftTIFA-AM) to Agree narrows the gap to VQAScore on GenAI-Bench from 0.15 to just 0.03 SRCC  (Table 2)  . This shows that expected agreement alone drives the improvement, while also raising NegBench accuracy from below chance to 88.3% without hurting performance on TIFA160. Merging takes the best of both. On all three correlation benchmarks Depict matches whichever term suits the benchmark and improves on it  (Table 2)  . The gain is significant on GenAI-Bench and positive but within the interval on TIFA160 and RichHF. The improvement comes from the low end: the merged metrics lowest-scored items are rated worse by humans than VQAScores on every benchmark and backbone, while the top tails coincide (Appendix D.3). The merge carries no penalty where one term suffices. On Winogrounds short compositional captions, the decomposed term adds little beyond what the holistic pass captures, keeping Depict within the confidence interval of VQAScore across all three accuracies  (Table 2)  . Furthermore, soft logit scoring across both terms (Agree) drives performance far more than decomposition itself, leaving discrete one-hot approaches like DSG lagging by 20 points. sections.title: 5.3 Why do agreement and merging work?
sections.content: In this section, we analyze how Agreement overcomes the structural flaws of fixed-yes rules on negation, while merging recovers performance on contested samples where terms disagree. The fixed-yes assumption fails on negation. By reading the expected answer from the caption, Depict is the only decomposed metric accurate across all three templates (Fig. 3a), while DSG and Soft-TIFA lose 8595% of their accuracy on negated items and fall below chance. This occurs because 87% of questions for negated captions and 47% for hybrid ones expect no vs 4% elsewhere (Appendix D.1), so fixedyes rule gives low score to every correct no before looking at the image, penalizing faithful images (Appendix B.2-B.3; text reference reliability in Appendix D.2). The terms are complementary. Agreement alone lifts both NegBench accuracy and human correlation over Faith but trails VQAScore on correlation; merging both terms places Depict ahead on both (Fig. 3b). The merge of both terms (Eq. 7) works because the terms fail on different samples: on GenAI-Bench they disagree on 19% of item pairs. Fig. 3c shows that Depict tracks the results where both terms agree and it follows whichever term separates the two images more strongly where they disagree. Depict keeps 65% of the pairs only the holistic term orders correctly and 54% of those only the decomposed term does. Whereas individual terms fail on each others exclusive wins, Depict achieves 60% accuracy across contested pairs, easily outperforming the holistic (53%) and decomposed (47%) terms alone. The merge relies on agreement: combining VQAScore with Soft-TIFA instead leaves GenAI-Bench unchanged and lowers NegBench to 62.2, below VQAScore alone, since the fixed-yes term drags down the holistic score on negated items (Appendix C.3). Along the Qwen3.5 ladder, Depict leads or ties at every size on all three correlation benchmarks, where larger backbones mainly narrow the gap for the weaker decomposed baselines. Across generations, its margins are largest on the newest backbone, Qwen3.8-27B, significant on four out of five benchmarks, even though that backbone scores below its predecessors for nearly every method.

sections.title: 5.5 Which components matter?
sections.content: Table 3 ablates the design choices of the decomposed term on Qwen3.5-27B, replacing one component at time while holding the rest at the final configuration and testing multiple scoring-rules. We ablate reasoning in the answering step in Appendix C.4. Tuple Extraction. Replicating DSGs tuple extraction hurts all benchmarks (Table 3a, top), 47% of negated NegBench captions yield no tuples and Negation-subset accuracy falls to 4.1, six times below chance, showing it cannot express absence. On Winoground pairs, which share entities but differ in structure, it generates overlapping questions (Jaccard 0.44 vs. 0.27 without tuples; 13% identical), shrinking the paired score margin by 40% and costing 21 group-accuracy points (Appendix C.1). Generating questions directly from the caption preserves both. Question pruning. Post-hoc pruning lowers performance on every benchmark. Earlier pipelines filtered questions to remove noise (Cho et al., 2024). Agreement scoring handles this per question: question the two channels cannot settle scores near the midpoint rather than being rewarded or silenced, and wk down-weights it (Appendix C.2), so pruning only removes questions carrying signal. Scoring. The scoring rule is the largest single factor (Table 3b), discretizing Faith as DSG does costs 16.3 Winoground points and 0.033 SRCC, while Faith stays below chance on NegBench. Agree raises it 4.6 and GenAI-Bench SRCC by 23%, moving Winoground by at most one point.

sections.title: 6 Conclusions
sections.content: Fine-tuned, holistic, and decomposed metrics each capture distinct part of caption-image alignment: fine-tuning aligns with human judgments but ties the evaluator to one backbone; holistic VQA preserves global context but misses fine-grained errors; and standard decomposition uncovers compositional logic but relies on fixed-yes target that breaks on negated captions. Depict resolves these trade-offs without training by evaluating two-sided answer agreement weighted by caption commitment, merged with holistic VQA pass. Agreement lifts NegBench accuracy from 19% to 88%, and the merged score matches or exceeds top evaluators across five benchmarks and eleven backbones. On DynEvals matched Qwen3VL-4B backbone, Depict beats DynEval-4B on GenAI-Bench (0.630 vs. 0.595 SRCC) and RichHF (0.607 vs. 0.546), though fine-tuning retains lead on TIFA160 (0.802 vs. 0.691). 8 Limitations remain: decomposition brings no gain on short prompts that hinge on compositional word order, such as Winoground, although enabling reasoning on answers improves results there; and because both channels share one backbone, prior shared by both can make the same hallucination look like agreement. Answering each channel with different backbone would decouple these priors, at the cost of hosting two models.

sections.content: Figs. 1117 show qualitative results for Depict on Qwen3.5-27B. Figs. 1112 trace the full pipeline on individual imagecaption pairs. The remaining figures cover the two selection tasks, choosing the image that best matches caption (Figs. 1315) and the caption that best matches an image (Figs. 1617), alongside VQAScore, Soft-TIFA, DSG, and the human judgments. In these examples, Depict selects the human-preferred image or the correct caption where the baselines do not, most clearly on explicit negation (Fig. 17, where only Depict selects the correct caption) and on attribute and spatial binding (Figs. 1415). Its scores are also graded, whereas DSG often assigns tied score of 1.0 to several candidate images. Fig. 18 shows two failures, one per selection task, and the per-question scores expose the cause of each. On NegBench #2034 the negation is handled correctly, since the text channel expects no bottle for the correct caption, but the image channel wrongly sees bottle (pv 0.7). This supports the distractor This image features bottle and contradicts the correct bottle is not shown, and because the holistic term makes the same perceptual error (0.41 against 0.15), Depict ranks the correct caption third of four (0.22 against 0.53). On GenAI-Bench #247, all methods prefer the Midjourney image, rated 4.0 by humans, over the DALL-E 3 image rated 5.0. Both terms of Depict favour it: the holistic term scores it 0.95 against 0.69, and in the decomposed term the two images differ mainly on whether the scroll is lit by the crystals, which the image channel affirms for Midjourney (agreement 0.98) but largely rejects for DALL-E 3 (0.35), while neither image is judged to show exactly two crystals.
